sentences.text: In the Allied Industrial Base the United States is the demand and market anchor, with a core seat in all ten strategic compacts.
It also supplies fab equipment, automatic controllers and AC generators, and it is the largest allied holder of gas liquids, refined fuels and gas-turbine and drilling components.
Nationally, its task is to keep the broad manufacturing base where it holds a top-quarter position, from battery cells and EV drivetrains to wind turbines and PV modules.
It should catch up where its position is below the top quarter but anchored: battery materials refining, reactors and nuclear fuel, and large power transformers.
The fence that matters is narrow: the rare-earth chain, the electrical steel inside transformers, and the control software of the battery systems it imports mostly from China.
It should source battery and EV minerals from trusted producers, and use development cooperation to add trusted capacity in EV drivetrains and battery cells.
Much of the map is left open: mining, fuels and basic processing are large, commoditized yards, and only battery storage and gas networks clear the bar for faster deployment.

The rare-earth chain from refining to traction magnets, where China holds 94% of world refining supply; grain-oriented electrical steel for transformers; and the firmware and communications of imported battery systems.
The answer is qualified trusted supply, stocks and control of command paths, not self-sufficiency.
Preserve the top-quarter positions in battery cells and components, EV drivetrains and vehicles, wind turbines and their parts, PV modules and inverters, and gas-turbine components.
Catch Up in battery materials refining, reactors and nuclear fuel, and large power transformers.
Source battery and EV minerals from Australia and Canada, where allied supply covers the need, and the wider wind-materials refining step from the allied holders Germany, Belgium and Spain.
Allied supply of that step falls short of need, so new capacity is also required.
With developing partners, development finance and offtake can add capacity in EV drivetrains and battery cells.
Accelerate battery storage and gas networks, with the market open to every trusted supplier.
Keep the Watch mining steps, fuels processing and grid components open.
Keep supply reliable in gas liquids, which allies rely on most, and in refined fuels, which they rely on less.

In Figure 1, color sits in the manufacturing columns, where the United States holds top-quarter positions, and in the nuclear chain, where it must catch up; mining, processing and deployment are mostly Watch.
The orange corner flags mark the High-fence parts: battery software, EV magnets and electrical steel.
Each cell is a supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in battery cells and packs, the battery software is Secure while the cells and enclosures are Preserve.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.
lack the data for a call.
Secure is a narrow call for the United States: one whole step and four layers inside other steps, which group into the three capabilities below.
Secure does not mean making everything at home.
It means being able to survive a prolonged cutoff or a hostile command, through qualified trusted supply, stocks, redundancy or control of the command path.
The core steel of power and distribution transformers, on which every grid expansion depends; it sits inside grid metals refining, a step otherwise left open.
Essential, import-dependent and slow to rebuild, in a step whose supply-chain need is 91; the need is measured for grid metals refining as a whole, not for the steel alone.

Stocks and spares pools sized to the rebuild time, long-lead procurement frameworks and capacity-reservation agreements with trusted producers; screening of foreign control of essential supply assets.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the traction motors of electric vehicles.
The United States holds 18% of world exports in the refining step's trade but only 1% of world supply, so the export share is a trade position to build from, not proven separation capacity.
China holds 94% of world refining supply and trusted suppliers 4%; substitution is hard and rebuilding takes more than three years.

Build separation and metal-making at home where a foothold exists; add trusted refining and magnet capacity with allies through co-investment and offtake; hold stocks until trusted supply qualifies, and phase in adversary-source restrictions as it does.
Battery-management firmware, energy-management software, gateways and cloud fleet management can command, update or disable storage from abroad.
China supplies 69% of US imports of battery cells and packs, and the control is built partly into the hardware.

Trusted-source and certification rules for firmware, communications and remote access; limits on remote access and over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors; a deadline to replace untrusted control in the installed base.
Where control is built into the hardware, trusted-source rules for that hardware and support for redesigns that separate the control layer.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
The United States holds a top-quarter position in eight high-value producing steps.

They are battery cells and packs; EV drivetrain components; EV and charger manufacturing; wind turbines; blades, towers and nacelle parts; battery components; PV modules and inverters; and gas-turbine and drilling components.
For most, need is low and the task is to stay at the frontier.
In battery cells and packs (need 90) and EV drivetrain components (73), keeping the position means expanding it, with support tied to benchmarks and the gate open to allied investment.
The magnets of blades, towers and nacelle parts read Preserve on that step's measures but Secure in EV drivetrains; this brief treats them as part of the rare-earth chain.
Battery materials refining is the best-anchored case for building: high value, a low position and five capability anchors, from operating capacity to committed investment.
China holds 94% of world supply, so trusted capacity here is scarce for every ally.
Reactors and steam generators, the highest-value Catch Up, and nuclear fuel and reactor parts rest on direct shares of world supply.
The AIB's separate measure of reactor parts, 18% of world exports or production, corroborates the reactor-parts side of both; it does not test fuel fabrication.
In transformers, switchgear and cables, where value only just clears the bar, the Catch Up sits in large power transformers, power conversion hardware and HVDC control.
Gas turbines and LNG plant and drilling rigs, tankers and oil equipment sit just under the top quarter (74 and 72): positions to keep competitive more than gaps to close.
This brief does not build on the Catch Up calls with the weakest anchors.
Uranium conversion and enrichment rests on a small share of world exports, about 1%, and on the position in fuel and reactor parts next to it; no conversion or enrichment capacity is measured.
Battery recycling rests only on a share of world exports (12%) of what the AIB analysis calls battery recycling feed.
Battery mineral mining and EV mineral mining have high need and no top-quarter position, and allied supply covers the need: source them from Australia and Canada.
In rare-earth and wind materials refining, allied supply falls short, and the recommended partners are Germany, Belgium and Spain.
Most of that step's trade by value is copper wire rod, not rare earths; its rare-earth separation layer reads Catch Up and belongs with the Secure chain, so partnering applies to the wider basket.
Some physical capabilities sit in several technology chains, and their calls differ because supply-chain need or evidence differs by technology.
The table keeps the national reading apart from what allies rely on the United States for.

Low fence — what not to prioritize
Watch is not a failure: it means affordable, diversified access matters more than domestic production.
Of the 25 Watch steps, 9 are deployment steps below the Accelerate bar.
Most others are large, commoditized yards in mining and basic processing, left open even where need is high.
Gas liquids processing and oil refining.
The United States holds 38% and 16% of world supply, the largest allied positions; in gas liquids it is a single point of failure for allies.
Keep them open: the obligation is reliable supply to allies, not a domestic fence.
Uranium, copper and bauxite, and PV mineral mining.
Need is high (99, 89 and 86), but these are large, commoditized yards.
The configured answer is diversified trusted imports and at most a limited, stated capability floor.
Drilling and pump components, coal-plant components and grid components.
Supply-chain need is low: buy competitively.

Every number comes from the Country page data of the Allied Industrial Base Explorer (the data release of 30 October 2026) and from the Allied Industrial Base analysis.
Each technology is split into six supply-chain stages, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches 60;
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (75) and either Strategic Industrial Value (bar 60) or supply-chain need (bar 67) is high;
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;
Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar.
Observed policy never decides a choice.

The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.
Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence.
They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.
